sector: Residential Property - Higher Yielding / Positively Geared
headline: Investors pivoting toward higher-yielding and positively geared residential assets as capital growth expectations moderate under new tax policy
reasoning: With the removal of negative gearing benefits for new investors in the established market and SMSF property lending shut down by policy makers, Andre Knott says investors are asking better questions and seeking better yields. He notes they are factoring in potentially lower capital gains over the next couple of years and therefore looking at neutral or positively geared residential assets. The shift toward positive gearing represents a meaningful change in investor behaviour rather than an exit from property altogether.
quote: Investors not not pulling out entirely, but they're actually just asking much better questions. They're looking probably for better yields as a result because they're factoring in that they may not have the same degree of capital gains across the next couple of years. So they're looking to invest differently, potentially into higher yielding residential property assets and some commercial property assets too.

headline: Established property investors holding assets and not divesting, banking on potential political sentiment shift ahead of state and federal elections
reasoning: Andre Knott observes that established investors are sitting on their assets rather than looking to divest over the next couple of years. Many investors believe market sentiment may shift politically, with state elections in Victoria and New South Wales and a federal election in 2028 potentially reversing some policy changes. Established-property holders can maintain existing capital gains tax and negative gearing benefits. At the same time, these investors are seeking to leverage existing equity into neutral or positively geared residential assets as a complementary strategy.
quote: What's happening at the moment is that the established investors, those who have been in the market for some time, um, as a lot of people are noticing in the marketplace, they are holding back and not holding back. That they're sitting on their assets. They're not looking to divest them across these next couple of years. I mean, a lot of people I'm speaking to are of the opinion that we're seeing a shift in, in market sentiment as far as from a political nature, which way they're going to vote and which way the populace may vote in the next couple of years, across state elections in Victoria and New South Wales, as well as in the upcoming federal election in 2028. And so they're holding their assets in established property because they can maintain those capital gains tax and negative gearing benefits.

headline: Andre Knott warns against investing in far-flung regional centres with narrow employment bases, citing personal mistakes over 27-year career
reasoning: Drawing on his own 27-year investing career, Andre Knott cautions against investing at the wrong stage of market cycles and particularly in regional centres where economic fundamentals rely on a single industry without sufficient employment diversification. He positions this as one of the most significant mistakes an investor can make, and advises clients toward safer transactions in more diversified markets.
quote: One of those mistakes or great mistakes I've made is investing at the wrong stages of market cycles, and also investing into far flung regional centers where, uh, the fundamentals are backed up only by specific industries. Um, and and not enough market differentiation in the employment sector, you might say. So what I what we work with our clients in is making sure they get into safer type transactions.

headline: Focus Property Group seeing 46% surge in investor enquiry as investors shift from established to new-build residential property following budget changes
reasoning: Andre Knott reports a 46% increase in investor enquiry over the last two months, contrary to media narratives of falling investor confidence. He attributes this to financial planners, brokers and accountants steering clients toward new-build property where capital gains tax and negative gearing benefits are still intact. Focus Property Group targets properties in the $650,000–$800,000 range, which is below the national median. Investors are also increasingly seeking higher-yielding residential and commercial assets given expectations of lower capital growth over the next couple of years.
quote: What we're finding is about a 46% increase in investor enquiry acquired during this period, um, just in the last two months. And we we're putting that down to, well, what we're experiencing is a lot of people investing or showing interest through financial planners, brokers, accountants, industry professionals that they trust, um, where they thought they may actually in, uh, look into the established market. But these industry professionals are saying, well, look, the opportunities still remain for capital gains tax benefits and negative gearing benefits in the new build sector, which is a market that we have as a business focused in on for the last ten years.

headline: Investors also eyeing commercial property assets as an alternative to established residential amid policy changes
reasoning: Andre Knott notes that alongside higher-yielding residential property, some investors are looking at commercial property assets as an alternative destination for their capital. This is framed as part of a broader diversification away from traditional negatively geared established residential property, driven by the new policy environment.
quote: They're looking to invest differently, potentially into higher yielding residential property assets and some commercial property assets too.

headline: Focus Property Group favours major Australian capital cities over regional centres, targeting early-stage growth cycles for mum-and-dad investors.
reasoning: Andre Knott advises positioning property investors in the five major capital cities — Melbourne, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth and Brisbane — as well as some regional capitals, rather than in far-flung regional centres where fundamentals depend on single industries. The key strategy is to get ahead of the curve in cities showing strong market sentiment over the next two to three years, enabling equity growth. Knott warns that investors who enter at the top of a market cycle can sit on a flat growth curve for five to seven years, limiting their ability to extract a deposit and reinvest. The typical client is a mum-and-dad investor holding one to three properties over a 10–15 year horizon, investing for retirement and intergenerational wealth rather than as a professional tycoon.
quote: What we work with our clients in is making sure they get into safer type transactions. I think it's important to realize that a majority of investors, property investors out there are, you know, besides what the government may have you believe or the policymakers may have you believe they're not rich tycoons. They're people who are investing in 1 or 2, possibly three investments across a long period of time. We're talking across ten, 12, 15 years. So we're looking to position them around the fundamentals of good quality property investing, particularly in major cities. The five big capital cities of Melbourne, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth and Brisbane. Some of the regional capitals as well are to diversify their investments, but making sure that we're looking to get ahead of the curve and look to see strong market sentiment in those areas across the next two years or three years, so they can actually have some equity growth rather than markets that have been really doing extremely well across the last 3 or 4 years, because we find that clients or investors who get in at that stage at the top of market cycles will sit on a fairly neutral type growth curve across the next five, maybe seven years.

headline: SMSF property lending ban and removal of negative gearing in established market are reshaping investor behaviour for at least the next two to three years
reasoning: Andre Knott highlights that policy makers have shut down the opportunity for SMSF lending into property for at least the next couple of years through to the next election. Combined with the effective end of negative gearing benefits for new investors in established property, these structural policy changes are the key drivers of shifting investor behaviour rather than a collapse in property demand. He expects these conditions to persist until political sentiment potentially shifts after state and federal elections.
quote: The government has now, or the policy makers have, have actually shut down the opportunity for lending inside an SMSF and for new for property, that is and um, across at least the next couple of years to through to the next election, that's going to be the case. So we've got people. Investors not not pulling out entirely, but they're actually just asking much better questions.
